A machine learning approach to analysis of Canadian provincial power 
system decarbonization 
Zahra Jahangiri
a , *
, Richard Hendriks
b
, Madeleine McPherson
a 
a
Institute for Integrated Energy Systems, University of Victoria, Victoria, BC, Canada 
b
Civil and Mineral Engineering, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada   
ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords: 
Provincial policy planning 
Decarbonization pathways 
Energy systems modeling 
machine learning 
ABSTRACT  
Canada committed to reducing national greenhouse gas emissions by 40 – 45 % by 2030 and achieving net-zero by 
2050, relying on low-carbon electrification across economic sectors. This study investigates the machine 
learning ’ s potential to analyze least-cost optimization of Canadian provincial power systems to 2050, to identify 
robust pathways for net-zero electricity system greenhouse gas emissions, and to provide policy insights 
respecting wind and solar generation, reducing emissions from natural gas generation, and expanding inter -
provincial transmission. Surrogate modeling is applied as sensitivities to generation technology capital costs, 
electricity demand, and carbon pricing to results from an existing capacity expansion mixed-integer linear 
optimization model. Under almost all future scenarios, six provinces develop new wind generation, with sub -
stantial deployment in Alberta (mean 27.3 GW, max. 62.7 GW), Ontario (mean 6.8 GW, max. 19.3 GW), Sas -
katchewan (mean 3.6 GW, max 8.9 GW) and Manitoba (mean 1.5 GW, max 3.5 GW). With the potential exception 
of BC, where higher-cost wind generation results in solar generation becoming the primary low-carbon electrical 
energy source (mean 25.2 GW), future solar generation across Canada is more limited (mean 37.1 GW) and less 
certain than wind generation in all other Canadian provinces. Existing natural gas generation is maintained in 
almost all scenarios in all provinces, providing support for maintaining these resources for reliability and reserve 
requirements. Very limited natural gas is developed under any scenarios, with the exception of British Columbia 
(mean 4.3 GW) where more than 80 % of scenarios include new natural gas capacity. Additional transmission 
transfer capacity is developed in most scenarios between BC-Alberta (~60 % of scenarios), Saskatchewan- 
Manitoba (~85 %), and Ontario-Quebec (~75 %). Carbon prices, along with wind and solar capital costs, act 
as primary determinants of least-cost decarbonization pathways. These findings offer insights for Canadian 
policymakers into net-zero pathways for provincial electricity systems that remain robust despite variability in 
inputs.   
1. Introduction and motivation 
As a party to the Paris Agreement, Canada committed to reducing 
national economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40 – 45 % by 
2030 ( Government of Canada, 2023a ) and to net-zero by 2050 ( Canada 
Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act, 2021 ). Achievement depends 
upon simultaneous end-use electrification, electricity generation 
decarbonization, and electrical technology evolution ( Vaillancourt 
et al., 2017; Arjmand and McPherson, 2022 ), necessitating expansion 
and decarbonization of the power sector. Decarbonization analyses of 
Canada ’ s electricity sector considering uncertainties in technology costs, 
electricity demand and effects of carbon pricing result in very large 
buildouts of hydroelectric, wind or nuclear generation ( Arjmand and 
McPherson, 2022; The Canadian Academy of Engineering, 2016; 
Bataille et al., 2023 ) or significant transmission expansions ( Dolter and 
Fellows, 2022 ). These studies focus on determining technically feasible 
or economically viable national strategies, an approach with disadvan -
tages for determining robust pathways to decarbonization considering 
policy uncertainties and model limitations. 
Since electricity services in Canada are provincially regulated,

provincial economies ( CER – Provincial and Territorial Energy Profiles – 
Canada, 2023 ), geographies, technology costs, and policy realities 
( Carbon pollution pricing systems across Canada - Canada.ca, 2023 ). 
Canadian provincial economies differ substantially in their sectoral 
contributions to gross domestic product (GDP) and in their per capita 
GDP ( Fig. 1 ). Contributions of the energy sector (i.e., oil, natural gas and 
coal production and distribution) to GDP range from a fraction (1.2 % in 
PE) to nearly a quarter (23.0 % in AB) of provincial economies, while 
contributing proportionately to provincial emissions and substantially 
(28.2 %) to national emissions ( Greenhouse gas emissions - Canada.ca, 
2024 ). The range in per capita GDP (~$42k in the Maritimes to ~72k in 
Alberta) reflects differences in consumer ability to finance the costs of 
electricity decarbonization ( IESO, 2023a; AESO, 2022 ). Some Canadian 
provinces have abundant variable renewable, hydroelectric, or nuclear 
generation while others rely heavily on fossil fuels, resulting in elec -
tricity sector GHG emissions intensities ranging from 1 to 670 
tCO
2
e/GWh ( Government of Canada, 2023a ) ( Fig. 2 ). Others face 
geographical constraints on development, lack access to low-carbon 
resources capable of integrating variable renewables (e.g., storage hy -
droelectric), lack high-quality geological storage sites, or require 
transmission expansion to integrate remote resources, all of which 
contribute to variability in the costs of electricity decarbonization ( Diner 
et al., 2023 ). 
Notwithstanding provincial regulation of the electricity sector, Ca -
nadian provinces are subject to federal regulations supporting national 
decarbonization efforts ( Government of Canada, 2024a ). These include 
economy-wide carbon pricing with an output-based pricing system 
(OBPS) to mitigate adverse effects on competitiveness ( Greenhouse Gas 
Pollution Pricing Act, 2018a; Output-Based Pricing System Regulations.; 
Government of Canada, 2024b ), phasing out conventional coal-fired 
generation by 2030 ( Reduction of Carbon Dioxide Emissions. ), and 
imposing performance standards (370 tCO
2
e/GWh) on natural gas-fired 
generation ( Regulations Limiting Carbon Dioxide Emissions. ). In addi -
tion, to limit remaining emissions from natural gas generation beyond 
2030 ( Arjmand and McPherson, 2022 ), pending regulations require 
net-zero provincial electricity systems by 2035 ( Government of Canada, 
2022 ). 
Canadian provinces implementing fossil-fuel generation phase-out, 
renewable portfolio standards, and feed-in-tariffs successfully reduce 
electricity sector emissions though, misalignment of federal and pro -
vincial policies could limit national emission reductions ( Jordaan et al., 
2017 ). For example, some but not all provinces prohibit nuclear ( Nova 
Scotia Power Privatization Act, 1992 ) or large hydroelectric develop -
ment ( Clean Energy Act, 2010 ), renewable energy and GHG reduction 
targets differ across provinces, while provincial carbon pricing regimes 
also vary despite the federal carbon pricing mechanism ( Carbon pollu -
tion pricing systems across Canada - Canada, 2023 ). Recent studies also 
indicate that least-cost decarbonization in some provinces entails 
development of inter-provincial ( Dolter and Rivers, 2018; Brinkman 
et al., 2024 ) and international transmission ( Brinkman et al., 2024; 
Rodríguez-Sarasty et al., 2021 ). Multi-year federal efforts aimed at 
securing substantially enhanced regional transmission in Atlantic Can -
ada ( Natural Resources Canada, 2022 ) recently concluded with pro -
vincial utilities opting for a more modest expansion of an existing 
transmission intertie ( Joint Policy Statement on Developing and 
Transmitting Clean, 2024 ). Provincial level analyses could provide 
planners and policymakers with in-depth understanding of the chal -
lenges and opportunities specific to each province, while producing 
deeper insights into policies for developing variable renewable genera -
tion, reducing emissions from natural gas generation, and expanding 
interprovincial transmission. 
The historic focus on pathway analysis also lends itself to electricity 
system modeling centered on least-cost optimization, simulation, and 
single-factor sensitivity. This conventional approach has limitations 
relevant to evaluating net-zero pathway robustness, which requires 
comprehensive examination of strategies and technologies in the 
context of uncertainties inherent to evolving and interconnected power 
systems. First, conventional approaches are computationally intensive, 
limiting available scenarios for exploring sensitivities associated with 
alternative futures. Secondly, these approaches typically assume deter -
ministic relationships between variable inputs and model outputs, 
limiting their application for decision-making under uncertainty. Power 
systems are subject to significant variability in technology costs, oper -
ations, policy constraints, and future electricity requirements, particu -
larly on the multi-decadal horizon of deep decarbonization. Thirdly, 
conventional models often exclude correlations between model param -
eters, and between parameters and input variables. In policy-setting and 
decision-making, such correlations are often salient to determining op -
portunities for implementing deeper, more cost-effective, or less risky 
decarbonization pathways. 
Machine learning (ML) models offer a potential solution to charting 
decarbonization of Canadian provincial electricity systems while ac -
counting for uncertainties and variabilities. A recent review of ML 
techniques demonstrated increased interest in using ML to address 
technical challenges in evolving power systems ( Ibrahim et al., 2020a ). 
These challenges in forecasting renewable energy generation and future 
deployment stem from multifaceted uncertainties inherent to wind 
( Nazir et al., 2020 ) and solar ( Alhamer et al., 2022 ) resources and to 
evolution of technologies ( US Department of Energy Wind Energy

Technologies Office, 2023 ) and costs ( Ramasamy et al., 2022 ). These 
uncertainties involve complex non-linear relationships between input 
parameters and outcomes, and the integration of real-world un -
certainties into modeling frameworks. Estimating rare events and 
extreme outcomes poses additional challenges due to their infrequency 
and impact. Moreover, long-term electricity system planning horizons 
and interlinked socio-technical factors exacerbate uncertainty, particu -
larly in detailed modeling of optimization strategies. 
By capturing complex correlations and relationships between model 
parameters and input variables, ML models account for uncertainty and 
variability in wind and solar generation ( Benti et al., 2023 ) and power 
system evolution ( Javed et al., 2022 ), supporting more robust decar -
bonization strategies that are optimal or near optimal under a wide 
variety of future conditions. In the context of the large datasets inherent 
to multi-factor uncertainty and variability, ML models can also be 
trained to learn patterns and relationships not apparent to conventional 
models ( Ibrahim et al., 2020b ). An exploration of ML techniques in 
power systems highlighted advantages and limitations compared to 
conventional techniques and concluded that ML offers significant po -
tential for real-time applications in power systems ( Miraftabzadeh et al., 
2019 ). ML methods have been applied to load forecasting and power 
system optimization problems ( Asgharinejad Keisami et al., 2021 ), to 
determining the importance of stakeholder and planning criteria in 
system expansion planning ( Majid Oloomi Buygi, Hasan Modir Shanechi 
et al, 2006 ), and to solving complex control problems in power systems 
( Zidong Zhang et al., 2020 ). A recent analysis utilized ML to integrate 
principal component analysis and clustering techniques to determine 
representative days for a reduced capacity expansion model applied to 
model grid decarbonization ( Zhao and You, 2022 ). 
These investigations demonstrate the potential of ML models to 
improve the accuracy and efficiency of power system planning and 
modeling, enabling more informed and effective decision-making. 
However, none of these studies explore the potential of ML in capacity 
expansion models to explore correlations, uncertainties, and variability 
in different input parameters affecting power system evolution. 
Exploiting the capabilities of ML methods in capacity expansion plan -
ning could improve policymaking and planning for decarbonizing these 
regional electricity systems ( Jahangiri et al., 2023a ). 
Contributions. Our contributions to energy systems modeling using 
ML models are as follows:  
• Analyzing robust least-cost pathways to net-zero electricity system 
decarbonization in Canada considering technology and policy 
uncertainties.  
• Investigating the potential of ML models to analyze provincial power 
systems for net-zero emissions in response to capital cost, demand 
and carbon tax uncertainties and variability.  
• Utilizing ML for sensitivity and uncertainty analysis in provincial 
power system variables, reducing computational costs. 
2. Methodology 
2.1. Model development 
An ML surrogate methodology is applied to COPPER, a capacity 
expansion mixed-integer linear planning model, to achieve a more 
efficient and comprehensive analysis of output variabilities. COPPER 
determines the least-cost mix of generation and transmission capacity 
for a specific time period while adhering to power system and policy 
constraints. The objective function minimizes total system costs 
including investment, maintenance, production, and carbon costs over 
the study period ( Eq. 1 ).

COPPER encompasses various optimization constraints, including 
those related to power balance, planning reserves, thermal generation, 
hydroelectric development, renewable generation, transmission expan -
sion, and energy storage. Inputs include forecasted electricity demand, 
existing and future transmission, existing and future generation, and 
federal and provincial environmental and decarbonization policies. 
Though valuable for evaluating the effects of carbon pricing and 
decarbonization policies on grid evolution, COPPER is computationally 
intensive, which limits its practicality for evaluating outputs under 
future uncertainties ( Jahangiri et al., 2023a ). 
The current study investigates key Canadian provincial electricity 
system decarbonization outcomes for 2050, encompassing carbon 
emissions, power generation technologies and capacities, and interpro -
vincial transmission capacity. These outcomes offer a comprehensive 
understanding of power system evolution under select input parameter 
variations, including carbon prices, demand growth, and generation 
technology costs ( Table 1 ). Ranges for input variables are based on 
existing legislation, consultations with subject matter experts, and 
extension of upper and lower bounds by ~25 %, as is common practice 
in sensitivity analysis ( Jahangiri et al., 2023a ). For example, existing 
carbon pricing legislation increases prices by $15/t/year from $65/t in 
2023 to $170/t in 2030 but is unregulated beyond that date ( Green -
house Gas Pollution Pricing Act, 2018b ). The lower bound envisions

2.2. Model training 
The COPPER model is employed using the input variables in the 
specified ranges ( Table 1 ). No constraints are imposed on transmission 
expansion between provinces, allowing a wide array of potential 
transmission expansion scenarios. Additionally, no target is imposed on 
emissions reductions, which decline in response to increasing carbon 
prices and policy constraints, evolving towards net-zero but not to zero 
emissions by 2050. The produced model output data are cleaned to 
remove outliers, and normalized to a common scale to enable fair 
comparisons without range distortion or information loss ( Eq. 2 ). Out -
puts having a variance of less than 0.001 are assumed to be constant 
(model noise) and ignored in the training process, ensuring a stable and 
trustworthy base for future analysis and interpretations.

The neural network is trained using a dataset of COPPER input and 
output samples. An empirical model development approach is employed 
to identify optimal hyperparameters for the model architecture. The 
selected architecture contains one linear and eight residual blocks, each 
consisting of two linear layers, two batch normalizations, two dropouts 
and two ReLu activation functions, with 128 neurons per layer. Batch 
size, learning rate, and dropout ratio values are 128, 0.001, and 0.5, 
respectively ( Jahangiri et al., 2023a ). 
The average R-squared value across the entire test dataset is reported 
in Table 2 , alongside training and test errors, and indicates a high 
goodness of fit of model predictions to test data. This approach ensures a 
comprehensive assessment of the model ’ s overall performance. 
In Table 3 , the model ’ s run-time and resource use are compared 
against COPPER, demonstrating a substantial decrease in computational 
cost and resource requirements. This efficiency enables more feasible 
scenario exploration by allowing for as many runs as needed. 
2.3. Output representation 
Once the ML model is trained, a sensitivity analysis reveals patterns 
of evolution in each provincial electricity system to 2050. All inputs are 
varied within the selected ranges ( Table 1 ) using Latin Hyperbolic 
Sampling, resulting in over 2000 scenarios. The surrogate model outputs 
consist of deployments or retirements of generation (in MW) within each 
province, or expansions in interprovincial transmission transfer capacity 
(in MW). The impacts of system parameters on the future development 
of generation and transmission across all sensitivity scenarios are 
plotted in histograms specific to each technology within each province, 
and in maximum absolute derivative plots of standardized outputs with 
respect to normalized inputs. Computationally demanding, these de -
rivative plots present normalized values demonstrating the relative 
impact of each input variable on the respective output value. Negative 
values indicate a negative correlation, positive values a positive corre -
lation, while absolute value represents the strength of correlation. By 
identifying patterns, this approach provides insights into the relation -
ships between input sensitivities and evolution of each provincial power 
system to 2050. These graphical approaches are further elaborated in 
the results presentation. 
2.4. Model limitations 
In conducting this study, several assumptions and limitations were 
considered. As a mixed-integer linear program optimization model, 
COPPER has several limitations relevant to interpreting the results of 
this analysis ( Arjmand and McPherson, 2022 ). While the methodology 
employed here imposes specified ranges on input variables, biases may 
persist due to rapidly changing circumstances related to decarbonization 
assumptions, electricity demand growth, capital costs, and technology 
evolution. To reduce computational burdens, COPPER also makes 
simplifying assumptions including treating, transmission and most 
generation technologies as continuous rather than binary integer vari -
ables. A more realistic characterization of generation and transmission 
development entails modeling contemplated projects with known ca -
pacities. This might best be achieved by a regional analysis of a subset of 
provinces in order to diminish computational burdens. COPPER also 
does not account for landscape characteristics that could preclude wind 
and solar development and may overstate development potential in 
some regions. COPPER also has a limited number of balancing areas, and 
for most provinces does not consider intraprovincial transmission 
expansion, which can be important to determining optimized decar -
bonization pathways. Finally, imports and exports are modeled exoge -
nously using historical data since future conditions are unknown, so 
significant changes to trade patterns would influence optimal decar -
bonization pathways. Future modelling could consider varying

Despite its advantages, the surrogate ML model approach also has 
limitations in addition to those associated with COPPER. For dataset 
generation, COPPER’s default constraints were applied to represent 
practical and non-contentious pathways. One key limitation is the po -
tential loss of granularity and accuracy due to simplified representations 
that do not fully capture nuances in the COPPER formulation. Secondly, 
the reliability of the surrogate model depends upon the quality and 
comprehensiveness of the training data, so extrapolating the model’s 
predictions beyond the training data could lead to unreliable results. 
Additionally, this ML model exhibits less sensitivity to parameters with 
relatively small nominal values when normalized, potentially leading to 
lower predictive accuracy for small-valued outputs in some provinces, 
which are not the focus of this analysis. Furthermore, as COPPER 
evolves and incorporates new features, this ML surrogate model will 
require retraining to maintain accuracy. Lastly, while the surrogate 
model provides predictive power, understanding the specific reasons 
behind its predictions can be challenging, which may impact its overall 
interpretability. 
3. Results 
This ML analysis produces abundant results, not all of which are 
meaningful. Findings are presented as national and provincial sum -
maries in terms of additions of renewable generation (wind and solar), 
additions and retirements of natural gas generation, and expansions of 
inter-provincial transmission. Results presented are mostly non- 
constant, meaning they vary across different input sensitivities since 
such results are generally of greater interest to policymakers (Jahangiri 
et al., 2023a, 2023b). For example, results respecting coal generation 
are omitted since this technology is rapidly retired in all provinces under 
all scenarios due to high emissions, moderate fuel costs, and increasing 
carbon prices. Selection of results focuses on key provincial pairings 
including British Columbia (BC) – Alberta (AB), Saskatchewan (SK) – 
Manitoba (MB), and Ontario (ON) – Quebec (QC), which comprise more 
than 90 % of installed generation capacity in Canada (Canada Energy 
Regulator, 2023b), and where transmission interconnection expansion is 
under active consideration by system planners in support of grid 
decarbonization. 
3.1. Renewable generation 
Table 4 summarizes results for modeled wind and solar development 
within each Canadian province. Existing installed capacities reflect 
current installations of utility-scale wind and solar generation and 
exclude planned additions. Wind generation currently operates in all 
provinces, while most provinces do not currently have installed utility- 
scale solar generation. Scenarios with no additional capacity reflect the 
proportion of modeled scenarios in which no wind or solar is developed 
to 2050. Mean and maximum additional installed capacity provide in -
sights into the magnitude of the potential buildout of these technologies 
to 2050 within each province. 
Findings indicate that six provinces (AB, MB, ON, PE, NL, SK) 
develop wind with high robustness, as reflected by the low proportion of 
scenarios having no additional capacity by 2050. In three provinces (BC, 
QC and NS) the extent of wind development depends strongly on inputs. 
Only one province (NB) lacks additional wind development due to 
anticipated low demand growth (Canada Energy Regulator, 2023b). 
Solar development occurs in all provinces but varies substantially by 
proportion of scenarios with no utility-scale solar development 
(4–91 %), by mean (0.1–25.2 GW) and by maximum (1.4–72.2 GW) 
developed capacity. Provinces developing significant wind (solar) re -
sources are less likely to also develop significant solar (wind) resources. 
3.1.1. British Columbia and Alberta 
In BC, wind energy development exhibits high robustness, displaying 
limited sensitivity to input variations, as more than half of the ~2000 
scenarios develop no new wind (Fig. 3). The y-axis on this histogram 
presents the count of scenarios returning technology deployment values 
within each bin across the maximum range of values. The x-axis contains 
normalized values in standard deviations from the mean, with negative 
values indicating scenarios where values fall below the average. Spe -
cifically, mean wind deployment in BC to 2050 totals ~4.3 GW 
(4344 MW), ranging between 0 GW in ~1100 scenarios up to ~49.4 GW 
(6 s.d.) in the most extreme scenario. This insensitivity to inputs implies 
a relatively stable path of limited future wind energy development in BC, 
a finding further explored in the Discussion. 
Contrastingly, solar energy development in BC is characterized by 
greater variability and uncertainty that is significantly influenced by 
policies and input parameters, including the carbon tax, future relative 
capital costs of wind and solar, and electricity demand in both BC and 
Alberta (Fig. 3). The derivatives plot illustrates the effect of each of six 
factors on solar generation in BC to 2050. The maximum absolute de -
rivative value indicates the steepest slope or the maximum change of 
one variable in relation to the other. Higher carbon taxes, higher wind 
capital costs and lower solar capital costs significantly increase devel -
opment of solar generation, with demand in either province and the

Wind energy is likely to play a substantial role in Alberta ’ s energy 
future regardless of evolving circumstances. Substantial new wind 
(mean ~27 GW) is developed to 2050, with larger capacity buildouts 
under a significant minority of scenarios ( Fig. 4 ). The carbon tax is the 
primary factor influencing wind development, followed by lower wind 
capital costs and higher solar capital costs. Despite variations in inputs, 
solar development in Alberta reflects lower sensitivity to input changes 
(and lower overall development) compared to wind energy ( Fig. 4 ). 
3.1.2. Saskatchewan and Manitoba 
There are wide variations in the quantities of wind developed in 
Saskatchewan and Manitoba ( Fig. 5 ). In almost all scenarios ( > 95 %), 
new wind generation capacity is developed in Saskatchewan 
( > 1000 MW) and in Manitoba ( > 500 MW) by 2050. In rare scenarios

3.1.3. Ontario and Quebec

feature of Ontario ’ s electricity system, influenced by increasing carbon 
prices, and relative capital cost differences between wind and solar

tion is developed in Ontario with mean development (~2.7 GW) indi -
cating a somewhat less robust path compared to wind development. 
In nearly two-thirds of scenarios, additional wind is developed in 
Quebec, though compared to existing installed capacity (~4 GW) mean 
development (~0.5 GW) is modest. As in Ontario, in a majority of sce -
narios (~60 %) new solar generation is developed in Quebec, though 
unlike in Ontario mean solar development (3.2 GW) exceeds mean wind 
development. The lack of development scenarios including either wind 
(34 %) or solar (42 %) in Quebec illustrates significant dependencies of 
wind and solar build-out on input conditions. Future wind generation 
deployment in Quebec is driven by increasing carbon prices, the relative 
capital costs of wind and solar energy, and to a lesser degree by demand 
in Quebec and in nearby provinces, while no single factor influences 
future solar deployment in Quebec or Ontario. 
3.2. Natural gas generation 
Findings for natural gas generation indicate pathways to deep 
decarbonization in all provinces do not retire these generating assets 
almost regardless of input variables (Table 5). This result is facilitated by 
the model’s lack of a hard constraint on emissions, which decline to net- 
zero but not to zero by 2050. Natural gas additions are limited to 
combined cycle generation, which has lower modeled capital and 
operating costs compared to simple cycle generation. For all provinces, 
with the exception of BC, natural gas additions are minimal with sub -
stantial additions occurring only under very extreme circumstances. 
This flexible thermal generation, along with hydroelectric generation 
across the country, supports integration of increasing quantities of 
variable renewable generation while providing contingency and reserve 
capacity. This indicates a robust pathway for existing installed natural 
gas generation to support decarbonization into the foreseeable future. 
In BC, in contrast to other provinces, there is significant (mean 
4.3 GW) expansion in new natural gas combined cycle generation. This 
consistent selection of new natural gas generation reflects its lower costs 
compared to other forms of dependable and flexible capacity, including 
hydroelectric generation and energy storage, and that nuclear genera -
tion is prohibited in BC (Clean Energy Act, 2010). Existing combined 
cycle generation under all scenarios and simple cycle under most sce -
narios (95 %) remains operational until 2050 (Fig. 7).

In the majority of scenarios, additional transmission transfer capac -

(~85 %), and Ontario-Quebec (~75 %), with modeled development 
varying under different input conditions. Influencing factors across 
provincial pairings include higher wind costs reducing transmission 
development, and higher carbon taxes, higher solar costs and, to a lesser 
degree, demand growth increasing development. A high carbon tax re -
sults in more rapid decarbonization in provinces with comparatively 
higher emissions intensities (AB, SK, ON), triggering more intercon -
nection with highly decarbonized neighbouring provinces (BC, MB, QC). 
Lower wind generation capital costs increase wind capacity, which re -
sults in larger surplus generation best utilized in neighbouring juris -
dictions by developing additional interprovincial transmission. As solar 
capital costs decrease, the installed transmission between provinces 
decreases, an intriguing result explored further in the Discussion. 
4. Discussion 
The principal purpose of this investigation is to provide insights for 
policymakers into least-cost, robust pathways to net-zero within Cana -
dian provincial electricity systems. Specific policy implications dis -
cussed below include those related to the federal Greenhouse Gas 
Pollution Pricing Act , Clean Investment Tax Credit and Clean Electricity 
Regulations , the recently announced Alberta renewables policy and the 
BC Clean Electricity Delivery Standard . A secondary interest is to inves -
tigate the potential of ML models to analyze least-cost optimization of 
power systems to net-zero emissions in response to uncertainties and 
variability in technology capital costs, electricity demand, and carbon 
pricing. 
4.1. Renewable generation 
Our findings indicate that four provinces need to plan for significant 
new wind development to 2050, including Alberta (mean 27.3 GW, 
max. 62.7 GW), Ontario (mean 6.8 GW, max. 19.3 GW), Saskatchewan 
(mean 3.6 GW, max 8.9 GW) and Manitoba (mean 1.5 GW, max 
3.5 GW), with other provinces also likely to see additional wind devel -
opment ( Table 1 ). Solar development occurs in all provinces but varies 
substantially in terms of developed capacity. The primary driver of 
deployment is the federal carbon tax, indicating that increasing the price 
on carbon beyond the 2030 date currently mandated in the federal 
Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act is indispensable to deep decarbon -
ization. Technology capital costs also play a prominent role in driving 
renewables deployment. The recently proposed Federal Clean Electricity 
Investment Tax Credit introduces a 15 % refundable tax credit for non- 
emitting electricity generation, including wind, solar and abated natu -
ral gas generation, as well as interprovincial transmission ( Chapter 3: A 
Made-In-Canada Plan, 2024 ). To support investment, this investment 
tax credit needs to be predictable while also responsive to the potential 
for periodic stagnation and for rapid declines in the capital costs of re -
newables, both of which characterize the historical costs trends for wind 
( Lantz et al., 2024 ) and solar generation ( Solar Installed System Cost 
Analysis, 2024 ). 
At the provincial level, Alberta has high suitability for both wind and 
solar generation, most (72 %) of the investigated scenarios suggest no 
additional solar capacity to 2050, and modest mean future solar devel -
opment (~3 GW) compared to wind (~27 GW) ( Fig. 3 ). This can be 
explained by the differing contribution of wind and solar generation to 
reserve requirements, which are more challenging to meet in a decar -
bonized Alberta grid given its limited supply of hydroelectric generation 
( Fig. 2 ). The estimated year-round effective load carrying capability 
(ELCC) of wind generation (16 %) in Alberta ( Annual Market Statistics 
Reports » AESO, 2023 ) makes a meaningful dependable capacity 
contribution to reserve requirements reducing the need for natural gas 
capacity. The estimated ELCC of solar generation in Alberta in summer

(20 %) and winter (0 %) means that solar makes no winter contribution 
to reserve requirements in Alberta, a winter-peaking system ( Annual 
Market Statistics Reports » AESO, 2023; AESO, 2024 ). This reserve 
contribution difference tilts the preference toward wind over solar 
generation in Alberta. Nationally, the ELCC of wind generation is typi -
cally 15 – 35 % of installed capacity with higher contributions in winter 
than summer ( BC Hydro, 2023; Annual Market Statistics Reports » 
AESO, 2023; IESO, 2023b ). Across Canadian provinces, solar generation 
makes no contribution to winter reserve requirements, though almost all 
provincial systems are winter peaking ( BC Hydro, 2023; Annual Market 
Statistics Reports » AESO, 2023; IESO, 2023b ). Wind generation thus has 
a larger impact compared to solar generation in reducing the need for 
higher-emitting load-balancing generation. Cost is not the sole factor 
determining whether to proceed with wind or solar generation as 
operational considerations are also relevant ( Government of Alberta, 
2023 ). 
Alberta recently placed a seven-month pause on utility board ap -
provals related to wind and solar facilities to conduct an inquiry into 
environmental impacts, site reclamation, and electricity system reli -
ability ( Alberta Utilities Commission, 2024 ). In response to inquiry 
findings, the Government of Alberta announced a prohibition on wind 
and solar development on Class 1 and 2 agricultural lands and on wind 
development within a 35-km buffer zone surrounding existing and 
future protected areas ( Government of Alberta, 2024 ). This recent policy 
direction would preclude wind, and to a lesser extent solar, development 
over large areas of Alberta not considered in the current analysis. 
Additional investigation should assess the implications of this nascent 
policy, which would make unavailable some lower cost locations for 
wind and solar development. As a result, a higher carbon price would be 
required to shift deployment towards renewables and away from natural 
gas, delaying decarbonization. The sum of modeled mean wind 
deployment across all provinces in the current analysis (~46 GW) vastly 
exceeds total existing installed capacity (~16 GW) ( Table 4 ). Realizing 
this deployment requires policy alignment across federal, provincial, 
and municipal governments incorporating best practices for collabora -
tive development that considers rural, agricultural, human health, spe -
cies protection and wilderness values ( Jeyakumar and Todd, 2024 ). 
Neither COPPER nor the current ML model account for these landscape 
variables that could preclude wind development. Future modeling could 
utilize the current ML model to test variations in land availability (e.g., 
parklands, agricultural lands, waterbodies, etc.) and consequent effects 
on generation technology deployment and system costs. 
In BC, solar generation may be poised for significant expansion under 
appropriate cost and policy conditions. Modeled mean solar develop -
ment (~25 GW) greatly exceeds modeled mean wind development 
(~4 GW), despite wind generation currently being the lowest-cost 
source of low-carbon energy in the province ( BC Hydro, 2023 ). Two 
factors potentially contribute to this result. First, requirements for 
additional generation in BC are delayed due to the Site C Project, a large 
(1100 MW, 5200 GWh/y) hydroelectric facility that enters the COPPER 
model in 2025. Since our modelling inputs include greater declines over 
time in the capital costs of solar generation compared to wind genera -
tion, this delay results in greater proportional solar deployment into the 
future. Additionally, prime solar development locations in BC are rela -
tively proximal to the existing transmission network, resulting in 
comparatively lower transmission interconnection costs. 
4.2. Fossil generation 
Provincial electricity system operators plan for significant emissions 
reductions by taking different approaches to retirements, operations, 
and renewals of existing fossil-fueled generation. The Ontario Inde -
pendent Electricity System Operator determined that natural gas gen -
eration provides dependable capacity, quick response, ramping 
capability, and reliability services while contributing to reserve re -
quirements ( IESO, 2023a ). This combination of characteristics is 
difficult to replicate, as comparable low-carbon generation resources are 
expensive and require substantial lead times, while storage and demand 
response would be required in unattainable quantities, leaving natural 
gas generation in operation beyond 2035 ( IESO, 2023a; IESO, Natural 
Gas Phase-Out Study, 2021 ). Furthermore, a rapid phase-out of natural 
gas generation in Ontario would result in frequent blackouts ( IESO, 
Natural Gas Phase-Out Study, 2021 ). Similarly, the Alberta Electricity 
System Operator found that pathways to net-zero by 2035 were highly 
uncertain, costly, and required verified emission offsets and widespread 
application of unproven technologies ( AESO, 2022 ). For its part, Hydro 
Qu ´ebec is planning to retain and gradually convert remaining natural 
gas generation to operate on non-emitting fuels so that operational 
benefits and contributions to reserve requirements can be sustained 
( Hydro Qu ´ebec, 2023 ). 
Contrastingly, BC Hydro is implementing a 100 % Clean Electricity 
Delivery Standard, which would see the phasing out of remaining nat -
ural gas generation by 2030 ( Government of BC, 2022 ), a strategy 
potentially at odds with the current study ’ s findings. While most 
modeled scenarios across all provinces ( > 90 %) see no new natural gas 
development ( Table 5 ), the current analysis indicates that least-cost 
decarbonization pathways develop significant natural gas generation 
(mean ~4.3 GW) in BC to 2050. This finding is consistent with a recent 
assessment of integrated continental electricity decarbonization, which 
found that natural gas generation continues to be developed to 2050 
within BC and Alberta ( Brinkman et al., 2024; NREL, 2021 ). A more 
recent study examining options for 100 % clean electricity in the US by 
2035 found that unabated natural gas combustion turbines provide a 
significant proportion (21 %) of system dependable capacity while 
generating a small proportion (4 %) of annual energy ( NREL, 2022 ). 
Though emissions from unabated generation can potentially be offset, 
there is a high-cost premium to decarbonizing the last portion of elec -
tricity sector emissions ( NREL, 2022 ). These collective findings suggest 
that advancing the 100 % Clean Electricity Delivery Standard in BC, 
which would decommission remaining natural gas generation by 2030 
while prohibiting new unabated generation ( Government of BC, 2022 ), 
should be preceded by thorough consideration of alternatives, including 
retaining and developing natural gas generation while investigating 
low-carbon fuels ( Canada Energy Regulator, 2023a ) and carbon offsets 
( AESO, 2022 ), to mitigate the effects of rapid grid decarbonization on 
system-wide costs. 
The current analysis models to the policy context in place at the time 
of modelling, while policy is rapidly evolving in response to decarbon -
ization imperatives. In August 2023, the Canadian government tabled 
Draft Clean Electricity Regulations (CER) which apply a revised emis -
sions standard (30 tCO
2
e/GWh) to interconnected fossil-fueled genera -
tion beginning on January 1, 2035, or 20 years following facility 
commissioning, whichever is later ( Government of Canada, 2023b ). 
More recently, Environment Canada suggested increasing the emissions 
standard to permit abated natural gas generation (i.e., with carbon 
capture and storage) that operates primarily as load-following or 
peaking generation, and therefore cannot meet such a restrictive stan -
dard ( Government of Canada, 2023b ). Consistent with these contem -
plated revisions, the current analysis illustrates robust pathways to deep 
decarbonization in which almost all existing natural gas generation re -
mains on-line, operating less frequently as the system decarbonizes. In 
this analysis, the carbon tax is the most influential factor affecting 
generation and transmission development and acts as the primary 
constraint on the retirement and deployment of natural gas generation. 
In terms of retirements, following 2035 the lower performance standard 
contemplated in the Draft CER would further reduce annual capacity 
factors at many existing facilities, potentially triggering retirements 
earlier than forecast in the current analysis. Considering the low capital 
cost of natural gas generating units, the Draft CER may also have the 
effect of triggering retrofits of existing facilities to operate on 
non-emitting fuels to achieve emissions reduction targets while main -
taining reliability. In terms of deployments, the current analysis does not

4.3. Transmission 
Results for interprovincial transmission development provide in -
sights into the complex interactions between carbon taxes, generation 
technology costs and electricity demand. Findings for the three pro -
vincial pairings investigated indicate that lower wind generation capital 
costs increase transmission development between provinces, while 
lower solar generation costs decrease development. Lower wind capital 
costs result in more wind deployment and larger daily and seasonal 
surplus generation, which is managed through exports to neighbouring 
jurisdictions facilitated by additional interprovincial transmission 
development. By utilizing the geographic variability in the wind 
resource across two provinces, transmission expansion enables exports 
during wind energy surpluses and imports during shortfalls. Contrast -
ingly, lower solar capital costs trigger more solar deployment and larger 
intra-daily surpluses most cost-effectively managed through shifting of 
load-following generation rather than by developing additional inter -
provincial transmission. 
Increasing electricity demand also influences transmission develop -
ment, though to a lesser extent than carbon taxes and wind capital costs. 
In general, demand in the province in which less wind development is 
projected has a greater influence on interprovincial transmission 
development. In other words, increasing demand in BC, MB, and QC 
influences interprovincial transmission development more than does 
increasing demand in AB, SK or ON. This result is unsurprising consid -
ering that wind generation creates surpluses best utilized by neigh -
bouring provinces but only if their demand justifies interprovincial 
transmission development. 
In the case of Ontario-Quebec transmission, solar capital costs in -
fluence the need for new transmission more than do higher carbon taxes, 
a unique result. Higher solar capital costs also increase wind develop -
ment in Quebec ( Fig. 6 ). As solar capital costs increase, it is preferable to 
incur the costs of additional transmission in order to trade more elec -
tricity between these two provinces. In the case of BC-Alberta, the factor 
analysis suggests a similar mechanism driving transmission develop -
ment as between Ontario and Quebec ( Fig. 8 ). The additional findings 
that wind development is preferred in Alberta and solar development in 
BC suggest that given lower wind capital costs, Alberta develops large 
quantities of wind along with transmission to support exports to BC. This 
is supported by the additional influence of demand growth in BC on 
transmission development between the provinces ( Fig. 8 ). However, 
given lower solar capital costs, the provinces each develop their own 
domestic resources, mainly solar in BC and wind in Alberta, without 
expanding interprovincial transmission. 
These somewhat complex interactions between solar costs, wind 
costs and interprovincial transmission development have implications

5. Conclusions 
This research investigates the potential of ML models to analyze 
least-cost decarbonization of provincial power systems across Canada in 
response to uncertainties and variability in technology capital costs, 
electricity demand growth, and carbon pricing. The study provides 
several insights into robust pathways respecting wind and solar gener -
ation, reducing emissions from natural gas generation, and expanding 
Canadian interprovincial transmission that remain robust under many 
uncertainties and variabilities. 
Findings indicate robust conditions for substantially expanded wind 
generation but less robust conditions for expanded solar generation in 
the decarbonization of Canada ’ s provincial electricity grids. Most 
provinces develop wind under almost all future scenarios, with the po -
tential exception of British Columbia, where higher-cost wind genera -
tion results in solar generation becoming the primary low-carbon 
electrical energy source. 
While Canadian policy is increasingly directed towards decarboniz -
ing electricity grids, our analysis indicates that existing natural gas 
generation is maintained but infrequently operated in almost all sce -
narios in all provinces, providing support for policies maintaining these 
resources for reliability and reserve requirements. Almost no new nat -
ural gas is developed under any scenarios, with the noted exception of 
British Columbia. Carbon prices, along with wind and solar capital costs, 
act as primary determinants of least-cost decarbonization pathways. 
Considerations for planners and policymakers involve optimizing the 
use of existing natural gas generation while also strategizing gradual 
phase-out of emissions in line with decarbonization goals and system 
reliability. 
In terms of interprovincial transmission, our findings indicate that 
provinces should proactively and strategically explore opportunities to 
enhance transmission transfer capabilities, ensuring efficient energy 
exchange to meet regional demands. This exploration, including po -
tential federal investment, should be cognizant of the influence of lower 
wind generation costs in increasing the development of interprovincial 
transmission as part of a least-cost pathway to decarbonization, and 
lower solar generation costs decreasing the need for interprovincial 
transmission. 
Recent analyses of pathways to deep decarbonization reveal signif -
icant future wind and solar development across Canada ( Arjmand and 
McPherson, 2022; IESO, 2023a; AESO, 2022 ) demonstrate that the 
extent of development within individual provinces is the outcome of 
factors considered in the current analysis, including future demand 
growth, relative technology costs, and decarbonization policies, 
including carbon prices. However, other potential factors not considered 
here include variations in the quality of the wind resource (i.e., wind 
speed) or solar resource (i.e., insolation), the distance from these re -
sources to load centers, the influence of landscape characteristics, and 
the costs of interprovincial transmission. Resource quality and distance 
to grid are inputs to COPPER and considered to be accurately quantified 
with limited potential for variation. Future modeling could further test 
the influence of variations in land availability and interprovincial 
transmission capital costs on grid decarbonization in Canadian 
provinces.
